chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Geopolitics for Markets

lessons.title: Power, Resources, and Alliances: The Building Blocks of Geopolitical Risk

body.text: Almost every geopolitical event that hits your portfolio is really a fight over one of three things: who holds power, who controls a scarce resource, or which side of an alliance a country stands on. Learn to spot which one is in play, and a confusing headline becomes a predictable category.

children.text: The previous lesson gave you the four channels through which a geopolitical shock reaches your portfolio: trade, energy, capital flows, and currency. This lesson goes one level deeper and asks a different question: what actually causes these shocks in the first place? Almost every geopolitical event you will read about in this course, whether it is a war, a tariff, or a sanctions regime, is driven by some mix of three underlying forces: power, resources, and alliances. Understanding these three well enough to spot them in a headline is what separates an investor who reacts to news from one who anticipates it.
Three Kinds of Power That Move Markets

Countries project power in more ways than just armies. For an investor, the useful distinction is not moral, it is about which kind of power is being used, because each one hits markets through a different channel.

cells: Hard power
Military capability and its actual or threatened use, troop mobilisation, missile tests, naval deployments
Russia massing troops on Ukraine's border through late 2021, well before markets fully priced in the risk of war
Economic power
Trade leverage, sanctions, control over payment systems, currency dominance
Removing Russian banks from the SWIFT payment network in 2022, freezing a large share of Russia's foreign exchange reserves
Soft and diplomatic power
Alliances, treaties, influence over international institutions and rule-setting
The US rallying G7 allies to coordinate a unified sanctions response rather than acting alone

children.text: Resources: What Countries Actually Fight and Bargain Over
Behind most sustained geopolitical tension is a resource that is unevenly distributed across the world, and therefore worth controlling, denying to a rival, or securing access to.

stats.label: Energy
stats.context: Concentrated in the Middle East, Russia, and a handful of other producers, which is why energy is the resource behind the largest share of market-moving geopolitical events

stats.label: Critical minerals and chips
stats.context: Taiwan's TSMC alone manufactures the large majority of the world's most advanced logic chips, making the Taiwan Strait a resource flashpoint as much as a territorial one

stats.label: Food and agriculture
stats.context: Russia and Ukraine together accounted for roughly a quarter of global wheat exports before 2022, which is why the war also became a food-price story

children.text: Alliances and Blocs Investors Should Recognise on Sight

Alliances matter to markets because they determine how many countries respond together when a shock happens, and how coordinated that response is. A handful of blocs come up repeatedly enough in market commentary that you should be able to place them instantly.

body.title: When Today's Major Blocs Were Formed

events.title: NATO
events.description: A military alliance of the US, Canada, and European members, built around the principle that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

events.title: OPEC
events.description: Founded by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela to coordinate oil production and pricing. Expanded into 'OPEC+' from 2016 by adding Russia and other non-member producers.

events.title: BRICS
events.description: Originally Brazil, Russia, India, China, joined by South Africa in 2010. Expanded further in 2024 to include new members such as the UAE, Iran, and Egypt, positioning itself as a counterweight to G7-led institutions.

events.title: The Quad (revived)
events.description: The US, Japan, India, and Australia revived this security dialogue after a decade-long pause, holding regular leader-level summits since 2021 largely in response to China's growing influence in the Indo-Pacific.

columns.label: Alliance-driven event
points: Multiple countries respond in a coordinated way, amplifying the market impact
Sanctions, trade restrictions, or military support tend to be broader and longer-lasting
Example: G7-coordinated sanctions on Russia after February 2022

columns.label: Bilateral event
points: Largely contained to the two countries directly involved
Global supply chains and commodity prices are usually far less disrupted
Example: a border skirmish between two countries with no major alliance backing either side

children.text: Flashpoints: Where Power, Resources, and Alliances Collide

A handful of locations show up again and again in geopolitical risk coverage precisely because power, resources, and alliances all overlap there at once. These are worth bookmarking, since a new headline about any of them should immediately trigger the framework from this lesson.

cells: Taiwan Strait
Advanced semiconductor manufacturing, US-China rivalry
A disruption could choke global chip supply, directly hitting Indian IT hardware and electronics-linked stocks
South China Sea
Shipping lanes carrying a large share of world trade, competing territorial claims
Disruption raises shipping costs and delays across Asia, including goods bound for or from India
Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East
The world's most heavily used oil transit chokepoint
Directly moves crude prices, and therefore India's import bill, inflation, and the rupee
Russia-Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank
Energy supply to Europe, global grain exports, defence spending trends
Combines the energy and food channels at once, which is why its market impact has been unusually broad

body.title: Which Flashpoint Would Hit Your Portfolio Hardest?
body.scenario: You hold a portfolio concentrated in Indian IT services companies and a couple of electronics component manufacturers. Tensions rise simultaneously at two flashpoints this week: a naval standoff in the South China Sea, and renewed military exercises near the Taiwan Strait.
body.prompt: Which of the two flashpoints is more directly relevant to your specific holdings, and through which resource does it travel?
body.modelAnswer: The Taiwan Strait is more directly relevant here. It is a resource flashpoint centred on advanced semiconductor manufacturing, since Taiwan's TSMC produces the large majority of the world's most advanced chips. A disruption there travels through the critical-minerals-and-chips resource channel straight into IT hardware and electronics component supply chains. The South China Sea standoff matters more broadly for shipping costs and trade flows, but is less specifically tied to this portfolio's chip and electronics exposure.

body.title: Bloc or Bilateral?
body.question: The US, Japan, India, and Australia hold a joint summit and issue a coordinated statement on Indo-Pacific security. Which term best describes this grouping?
body.explanation: This four-country grouping, the US, Japan, India, and Australia, is the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, known as the Quad. OPEC+ is an oil-producer coordination group, BRICS is a bloc of major emerging economies, and NATO is a North Atlantic military alliance, none of which match this specific membership.

body.title: Power, Resources, and Alliances: Key Terms

cards.definition: The use or threatened use of military force or coercion to influence another country's behaviour.
Using trade access, sanctions, tariffs, or control over payment systems as tools of foreign policy, rather than military force.
Raw materials like rare earths and lithium that are essential to modern technology and defence manufacturing, but concentrated in production among only a few countries.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries plus a group of allied non-member producers, including Russia, that coordinate on oil production levels and pricing.
The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue between the US, Japan, India, and Australia, focused on Indo-Pacific security and countering China's regional influence.

points: Nearly every geopolitical event driving market moves can be traced back to a mix of three underlying forces: power, resources, and alliances

Power comes in three forms relevant to markets, hard (military), economic (sanctions, trade, currency), and soft or diplomatic (alliances and institutions), and each hits your portfolio through a different channel
Resources worth watching are concentrated and unevenly distributed: energy, critical minerals and semiconductors, and food and agriculture
Alliances matter because they determine how coordinated and broad a response to a shock becomes; alliance-driven events tend to hit markets harder and longer than purely bilateral ones

A small set of flashpoints, the Taiwan Strait, the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Russia-Ukraine-NATO region, recur because power, resources, and alliances overlap there simultaneously

body.text: Figures on resource shares, chip manufacturing concentration, and bloc membership are approximate and can shift as production capacity, alliances, and geopolitics evolve. Verify current figures and membership before using them in any investment decision.
